name: The thing-in-itself (noumenon) and phenomena
plain_explanation: What actually exists, causing our sensations, is unknowable ('the thing-in-itself'); what we actually perceive ('the phenomenon') is a joint product of that unknown cause plus our own mind's built-in ordering apparatus (space, time, the categories).
precise_definition: Noumena or 'things-in-themselves' are the unknowable causes of sensation, not in space or time and not describable by any of the twelve categories; phenomena are what appears in perception, consisting of a sensory component contributed by the object and a formal component (space, time, category-structure) contributed by the perceiving subject.
why_it_mattered: It is the load-bearing but, per Russell, deeply inconsistent element of Kant's system: things-in-themselves are treated as causes of sensations even though causality is supposed to be merely a category applicable only to phenomena -- an inconsistency Russell calls 'not an accidental oversight' but 'an essential part of his system.'
examples: Free volitions treated by Kant as causes of occurrences in space and time, despite causality supposedly being confined to phenomena
objections: The application of the category of causation to things-in-themselves (as causes of sensation, or as the ground of free will) directly contradicts the doctrine that categories apply only to phenomena.
influence_on_later_thinkers: Fichte and the successors abandoned the thing-in-itself altogether, moving German philosophy toward near-solipsism until Hegel sought a new, non-subjectivist escape route.
